utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Zagreb. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Mucic. My co-counsel is Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. Together with me is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, and along with my co-counsel, Cynthia McMurrey, we appear on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. I would like to ask permission of the court for Ms. McMurrey to leave the Trial Chamber at about 12.45 today. I believe she will return for the afternoon session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are still leading your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the witness? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please inform the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. MILOVAN KULJANIN (continued) Examined by MR. NIEMANN (continued)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, yesterday afternoon, just prior to the adjournment, you were telling us about incidents that you had observed during the period of time that you were detained in the Celebici camp. I was asking you about particular incidents that you saw. During the time that you were there, did you know or come to know a person by the name of Nedeljko Draganic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to Nedeljko Draganic when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions in building number 6 he was maltreated, beaten, abused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself observe this maltreatment and abuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, inside the building number 6 in which I was, I was able to observe when he was beaten on various parts of his body with various instruments and he was also kicked and punched. He was also burnt. I think that gasoline was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who it was that kicked and punched him inside hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly done by guards of the building, Esad Landzo, Osman Dedic, Esad Macic also on one occasion, and many others whom I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a time when he was burnt. Did you see him being burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it happened outside in front of building number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw the wounds on his legs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Mr. Draganic received medical attention for these burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether he received it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9th December 1992, that was when I was transferred to the Musala prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained in the Musala prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was there for a total of 880 days until 6th October 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Musala prison, were statements taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you left the Musala prison? Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was exchanged in Sarajevo at the bridge in Grbavica and then I went to Serbia, I spent about two months in Belgrade and then I spent ten months in Subotica and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the Musala prison and went to Serbia did you give any further statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement in Visegrad in 1996 or 1997, I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the purpose of that statement was? Do you know why it was that they wanted the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought because they wanted to have a clear idea as to what happened in the camp itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at this document that I am now going to show you and might it be marked for identification with the next Prosecution exhibit number in order, please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Prosecution Exhibit 175.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, could you just look through that document, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot read this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are some parts which are illegible, but the parts that you can read, just look at those for me. Can you see a date at the very beginning of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is 12th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your signature anywhere on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does your signature appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just answer my question if you can: do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am hardly able to read this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. What did you want to say? Mr. Kuljanin, it is not necessary for you to read the whole document at this stage. I just wanted you to tell me if you could whether or not it was your signature and whether you remember affixing your signature in about 12th June 1992 to a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am receiving interpretation in French. I have been hearing French for the past five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, can you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that I have just given you, can you see your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the circumstances of how it was that you came to affix your signature to that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has been complaining that the document is illegible. Do you think he should continue to say anything about such an illegible document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I apprehend, your Honour, that he is going to be cross-examined about it. I am not tendering this document, I am merely asking him the circumstances about how he came to affix his signature. If he is able to recognise his signature he may be able to recognise the circumstances under which he affixed it. The document is not entirely legible, but there are large portions of it which may assist him in that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he is not tendering it as part of the Prosecution's case, what relevance does it then have to the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not tendering it, your Honour, and that will emerge --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The objection I have is that it is not therefore relevant and therefore not admissible at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have not sought to tender it, your Honour. I am allowed to ask questions about a document during the course of it being identified and I am doing it. My friend well knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What matters is we are wasting everyone's time by bringing in the issue. Even if he said he affixed his signature to the document, to what does that document refer? It goes to no issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, all of these documents tend to be somewhat illegible, but so long as they are not used by the Defence, I have no objection, I will not proceed with any further questioning on them. It suits me not to take it any further, so long as the Defence do not do the same thing. If they stand up and start to cross-examine on the documents, then I will be putting strenuous objections to it on the basis that there should be some equality in the approach to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They could not if he can not even read it and nobody can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just say, there is no agreement by the Defence that we will not question with regard to this document, but the problem that Mr. Niemann is facing at this point is he is asking the witness to describe the circumstances of a document which the witness cannot identify because he cannot read it. So the cart is getting before the horse. If the witness says "yes, I can identify this document, I recognise it" then perhaps he can take the next step. As long as it remains a document the witness cannot recognise, then it makes no sense to ask questions about the circumstances under which it was prepared. That is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has already taken the hint and he is not tendering it. He is not even using it. I do not see the relevance of the objection at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I note that at least Mr. Ackerman for the Defence has said that there is no agreement. I was not seeking agreement, I was seeking quality of treatment. Your Honours, I will not pursue further this questioning on these particular statements, but the moment the Defence seek to do so, I will be left with no option other than application to reopen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Unless they can make the witness to be able to read it and be able to identify it, then that is -- if he still cannot and says he cannot read it and not remember anything about it, I do not see anyone can use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honour. Your Honours, perhaps I should just ask that question and if he is unable to identify it, then that is the end of the matter. Mr. Kuljanin, are you able to identify the document that you have now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can identify only my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a series of other ones which are more legible, your Honour. I will ask him to look at those under the same conditions, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have English translations of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are English translations, your Honour, but there is no point in showing the witness English translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I will provide your Honours with English translations. (Handed). Might the witness be shown this document? It need not be marked, because if the witness does not recognise it then I will not proceed to tender it. If he does recognise it then I will have it marked for identification. (Handed). Mr. Kuljanin, would you look at the document you are now shown -- it does not need to be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any part of that document that you recognise, Mr. Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the date on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15th January 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement at or about that time? Just look at the document that was handed to you, not that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not made in the premises of the Konjic police, it was made in the Musala camp itself. That is the only difference, but I remember the occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the statement was taken, were you given an opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to make any corrections to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody even asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you subjected to any threat or inducement when that statement was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as usual, we were maltreated every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this during the period of time that you were being maltreated, that this statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will have that marked, your Honour, with the next number in line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, I have three copies of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. We had several copies taken.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is 15th January 1994, all three copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is 7th February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They need to be sorted, your Honour. They need to be sorted out. They have been given to you all as one bundle. Might that document be marked with the next number in line ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 176.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, would you look at the next document I show you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am waiting for it to arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That need not be marked for the moment. Just give it to Mr. Kuljanin, please. If Mr. Kuljanin recognises it, we will mark it. If he does not, I will take it back. Mr. Kuljanin, is there any part of that document that you can recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a date on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7th February 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember giving a statement around 7th February 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7th February -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Musala, in the Musala camp, in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, same as for all the previous statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I might repeat the question just for the sake of the record, because it is not clear. Were you given an opportunity to read that document before you affixed your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, same as for all the other documents, the previous two statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given an opportunity to make any corrections to the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody even asked me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you under any threat or inducement when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I could say that there were several factors that had an impact on the actual giving of the statement. First of all, all of us who would not give the statement as they wished us to would definitely be beaten up beyond the point of being able to sit down on a chair for ten days, and anyone being asked what to write and what to say, there is no need to even talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that document be given the next Prosecution number in order, please? Might the witness be shown this document? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there can be a correction on this document, it says that I was brought to the prison on 9th -- at the end of September 1992. That is the only thing. It speaks enough for itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document that I show you, would you look at that document, look through it and tell me whether you recognise any part of document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only some of my words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise apart from the typed words any other part of the document? Do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date that is shown on that document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 12th April 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were on 12th April 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the Musala prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave that statement again, were you given an opportunity to read it before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, were you given an opportunity to correct it, correct any errors in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody even asked me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, were you subjected to any inducement or threat when you gave that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same as for all the previous ones. We knew what would follow if one does not speak the way they want you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might that document, the statement of 12th April 1994, be given the next exhibit number in order and might I enquire whether the previous one, the document of 7th February 1994, whether that was given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The previous one was 177 and this one is 178.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we know that the learned colleague does have documents available, documents that we have, but it would be good before the document is presented to the witness for the Defence to have an insight, or at least to see exactly which document it is, because this way we are discussing documents that we would not know the content of until the very end of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the correct procedure, your Honours, is once I ask for it to be marked for identification it should then be shown to the Defence, but I have no objection to the Defence to look at it now before he looks at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think he will show it to you before it is actually tendered. When he wishes to introduce it for tendering, he will pass it round to the Defence and then you will know why it is being tendered. What he is doing at this stage, as you notice, is for the witness to identify the particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add to this, for the past few months, we have been implementing a certain procedure and we have been building a way of presenting documents. When Defence wishes to use any document, it is first given to the Prosecution and then to the witness. I believe that in this way we could also do this in cases when the Prosecutor wishes the witness to identify a document. If again your view is different, then we should know so that we could proceed in a similar way when presenting documents to the witness for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually my view is not different. What prompted these procedure is because the first document the witness was unable even to read the document, he was not sure really whether he could identify it. The moment it was identified, I think the obligation to pass it round remains, so it is the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In view of what your Honour has said, might the Registrar kindly pass to the Defence the documents that have been numbered so they can look at those documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have received the indictments, but they are all mixed up, so I am unable to identify them and sort them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can give 176 to 178, the three documents could be passed round.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, do you recognise any part of the document that has now been placed in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know this document entirely. I know the whole document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances of that document being created?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited by the investigators to give a statement for the documentation centre and the Association of Detainees in Belgrade and that is this statement. I gave the statement in the court building of the Visegrad municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date is shown on that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 3rd February 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your signature affixed to that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you permitted to read that document before you affixed your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you permitted to make any corrections to the document before you affixed your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but there was no need for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any threat or inducement held out to you when you were asked to give this statement and sign that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly not. I gave this statement voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might this document, the one of 3rd February 1996, be given the next number, Prosecution number, in order and might it also be shown to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is registered as Prosecution Exhibit 179.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have arranged the exhibits, kindly pass it round to the Defence so they have their own copies. (Pause). I think this is the end of the Prosecution's examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope the Defence does not mind if we have a break for 30 minutes, and by the time we come back I am sure the exhibits will have been sorted out and you can have all the exhibits. We will come back at 11.15. (10.45 am) (A short break) (11.15 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olujic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If it may please the court, my colleague Michael Greaves will be absent in the first part in order to prepare the Defence so I will be by myself in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before I begin, may I raise one matter? There is confusion on this side of the room as to whether the Prosecution has an additional witness after this one or not. There was a misunderstanding in the communication yesterday, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The position at the moment, your Honours, is that the witnesses that we had planned for this week, the three additional extra witnesses have fallen through, they will not be available and will not come to The Hague at the moment. We have arranged to bring in one witness -- excuse me a second. (Pause). The witness is in fact -- we have one witness flying in at the moment, it is anticipated he will arrive here tonight. He is the last name on the list that we have already provided to the Defence for this week. The answer to the question is we do expect to have one additional witness this week other than this one. Other than that, all the other witnesses have refused to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that clear to the Defence now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that is not a protected witness, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it the intention of the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber to take that witness prior to the handwriting and the documents from Vienna, or to do those first and then put on that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The intention, your Honours, was that we would proceed with the legal argument and if there was time left, we would call that witness. If the legal argument consumes all the available time for the rest of the week, which we doubt will be the position, we would then call the witness. It was not our intention to seek to delay the argument on admissibility whilst this witness was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is perfectly acceptable, your Honour. That is what we had anticipated. We just wanted to make certain that was the position of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have two legal arguments before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are two arguments, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The order we have decided perhaps will be different from what you intend to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we call the witness for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the order of cross-examination will be Landzo, Delalic, Mucic, Delic. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I am reminding you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The cross-examination may continue. Cross-examined by MR. ACKERMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman and I will be asking you some questions here for the next several minutes, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I ask for the first couple of questions that I want to ask this witness that we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will go into private session now. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are. Thank you, your Honour. How many times have you discussed the experiences you had in Celebici and the period of time leading up to that and subsequent to that with Dr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have spoken to Dr. Jovanovic only about my health problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he has no knowledge about your experiences in Celebici other than what he might have heard sitting here in the courtroom listening; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, your Honour. (Pause). Does this doctor have any kind of a speciality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his speciality is psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were also with another witness who has testified here this week by the name of Rajko Draganic, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Draganic before your arrival here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you knew him even before your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that the two of you are close friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not very good friends, but we do know each other well enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suspect at some point you and he have discussed your separate experiences with regard to the war and Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We rarely talk about it. There is no need because we both know very well what we experienced. He has got nothing new to tell me and I have nothing new to tell him. That would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one thing that the two of you do have in common is that you were both witnesses here in the International Tribunal this week, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a matter of the court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a kind of extraordinary experience for both of you to go through, to be called here as witnesses and to be questioned and that sort of thing, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not understood the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an extraordinary experience in both your life and his to be called here as witnesses to testify before the International Tribunal; it is something neither of you have ever done before, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, naturally we knew that some day we would be coming here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that the two of you have come here, and have spent some time together, certainly you have talked about your experiences as being witnesses before this Tribunal with each other, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the time you have spent together here, what you want us to understand is that you have not spoken to each other at all about testifying before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that we have not discussed things about the court, but we did not talk about what happened to whom, because we know very well exactly what happened to whom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Draganic not tell you some things about his experience as a witness here being cross-examined and kind of help you understand what that might be like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in as much as that the court is fair and that there are no problems in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the only thing he told you about his experience here as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not have any discussions with him about it because someone told you not to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly not, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no one told you that you should not discuss anything with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that I am not supposed to talk to him, but as I say, we did not discuss anything about the court itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is it you know that you are not supposed to talk with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who gave you those instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we received them from the interpreters. Who gave them to them, that I do not know, as to how to act in the court, et cetera, what the rules of the court are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those things that you were told by the interpreters, one of those things were that you were not to discuss your testimony with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was: were you told by the interpreters that you were not to discuss your testimony with other persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I now want to ask you a series of questions about the various statements you have given. I would ask you to listen very carefully to my questions. I am going to try to phrase them in such a way that you can answer them with either a yes or a no; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please understand that if I want you to explain something about a statement, then I will specifically ask you to do so, but in most of the questions I ask you I am not requesting an explanation, but simply an acknowledgement of whether or not a statement was made, whether or not you have seen it before, things of that nature to which you can answer yes or no, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that there are several statements in existence which contain your signature because you have just seen several of them here in the courtroom, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, here in the courtroom, is not the first time, is it, that you have had an opportunity to see those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the first time or it is not the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have seen those statements before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The questions that Mr. Niemann was asking you about some of those statements, basically the statements that you gave at Celebici and while you were in Musala, one of the questions he was asking you about all those statements was whether at the time you signed them you had had an opportunity to review them before you signed them, and I think your answer to each one of those questions, with regard to each one of those statements, was that you had not; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did have an opportunity, did you not, on 23rd February 1996 to review all those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not all of them, the statement I gave on 23rd -- on 2nd -- on 3rd February 1996. That was the only statement that I had the opportunity to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also the one you gave on 7th February 1994 that was shown to you at that time, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me to see?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, for you to see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In 1994? Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed a statement that you gave to Ms. Sabina Manke of the office of the Prosecutor on February 23rd 1996, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ms. Manke give you an opportunity to learn what was in that statement before you signed it, or was it another situation where you were basically forced to sign it without knowing what it said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had full insight into the statement on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if that statement says that you had had an opportunity to review the statements given to Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities on 7th February 1994 and the one in Visegrad on 3rd February 1995, are you now saying that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. Which authorities in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that you gave to Ms. Manke refers to a statement you gave to Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities on 7th February 1994. Are you familiar with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that statement in Konjic, not in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That statement was shown to you by Ms. Manke when you talked with her on 23rd February 1996, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I said the same thing I said now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and with regard to that statement and the statement that you made in Visegrad on 3rd February, with regard to both of those, you were given the opportunity by Ms. Manke to correct anything in those statements that was wrong, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the statements from 1994?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 7th February 1994 statement and the 3rd February 1995 statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I corrected the one from 1994 and 1995, there is nothing to correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am trying to -- it is actually a 3rd February 1996 statement, not 1995. There is an error in Ms. Manke's statement, I think. Both of those statements were presented to you at that time and you were given an opportunity to review them and say whether or not there were things in them that you thought were incorrect so that you could correct them; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I did say what the things were that were not correct and I think that it was corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is not so, that was not my mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By my count, you have given nine statements regarding your experiences during the war, some dealing with Celebici, some dealing with other matters. Have you made a count so you know that is the number you have given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think there were nine. I know about four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about a video statement that you made regarding your experiences in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: More than one of those, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not know. Who knows how many times I was taped? I could have been taped 100 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, of course, have seen today and you recall a statement that you gave on 12th June 1992, that is the first exhibit that was shown you by Mr. Niemann and the one that you said you really could not identify anything but your signature; you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that would be a statement that you gave very soon after arriving at Celebici when you were questioned by Kuhar and Miro Stenek?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question. If the witness said he cannot identify it, then how can he now give evidence about what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You did give a statement around 12th June to Miro Stenek and Kuhar, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mid June, when I arrived. That was the first statement I had given in Celebici, in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave another statement on 12th January 1993 after you had gone to MUP and you have seen that statement this morning, have you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not go anywhere. They came to the Musala prison where they conducted interviews with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there may have been a mistake in the translation. That is what I had suggested, that this was a statement you gave in Musala after you had been transferred there on 12th January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not on 12th January, it was on 9th December that I was transferred from Celebici to Musala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but after that, on 12th January you gave another statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise to mention a couple of points. When my friend was referring to the statements from the Office of the Prosecutor, he was saying it was a statement of 23rd February 1996, when in fact it was a statement that the witness gave on 14th November 1996. He now keeps referring to a statement on 12th January and I think it is the 15th, if he looks at it. I do not know of any statement on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is mass confusion at this point. I have a statement that was given me by the Office of the Prosecutor made January 12th 1993. Maybe Mr. Niemann does not have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher to give it to Mr. Niemann? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not yet in evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, apparently the Prosecutor's office, after giving it to us, lost it. Just a minute. (Pause). I am sorry. Show it to Mr. Niemann. (Handed). I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does my friend still maintain it comes from the Office of the Prosecutor, because it is not a document that certainly I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have just been informed that it did not come from your office, it came from elsewhere. I would ask that the Serbo-Croatian version of that, your Honour, in the same manner that Mr. Niemann did it, be shown to the witness to see if he can identify the document, before it is marked, please. Please do not mark it until he says whether he can identify it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have to mark the documents before deciding whether the document will be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a moment ago Mr. Niemann was permitted to show documents to the witness for identification before they were marked to see if he could identify them. We understood the procedure was they all had to be marked before showing to the witness but that procedure changed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The procedure did not change. What I explained immediately after Ms. Residovic complained about it, because he was unable to identify it, he could see whether he could identify it or not. In the normal procedure, the Registrar marks every paper that passes through and then sends it to the witness. Whether it is finally tendered or not, it still has a Registry number, even if it is withdrawn, it has a Registry number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That has been my understanding until this morning, when Mr. Niemann was asking they be shown to him without being marked, and was permitted to do that. I do not have any objection to this being marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, that is a complication. As I said this morning, the witness was protesting that it was illegible. If it is illegible, there is no point in even showing it to him. Finally I do not think he even proceeded to show it to him because I explained that there was no point, he cannot identify what is illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no complaint about it being marked. They may go ahead and do that and then show it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I was only referring to a precedent which is now thought to have been made, but that was not a precedent as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no problem with it. I just want to have it understood that that will be the rule from now on, no matter what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Not interpreted).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got no translation of what was just said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Defence Exhibit D25/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kuljanin, you now have before you a statement. My first question is: do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it have your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does have my signature, but the contents are not mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the incident, the time that that statement was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just check the date. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave a statement dated 15th January 1994, did you not, that was shown to you this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave a statement dated 7th February 1994, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a statement dated 3rd February 1996 to the investigating judge in Visegrad, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a statement dated 23rd February 1996 to the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I skipped the April 1994 statement that you gave that was Exhibit 178 from this morning, you remember that one, of course? Do you remember that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was April 1994, it is exhibit number 178, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on 14th November 1996, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By my count, that all adds up to nine if you count the video statement that I had mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By my count, that is nine statements if you count the video statement that I had mentioned earlier that you agreed there was at least one of and perhaps more; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe even more. There were more statements, but this is what we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you given -- you have given more statements that are not present in the courtroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would sometimes give one or two statements a day. It may have been 50 statements or even more. It is not just me, all of us there who spent a long time there were in such a position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have talked about a statement that you gave to an investigating judge in Visegrad on 3rd February 1996; you remember that statement, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you told us that that statement was given basically at the request of the Association of Detainees in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you gave that statement to a judge in a court? Do you know why it was done that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was for the purpose of collecting evidence about war crimes that had been committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it was also for the purpose of making certain that you were advised of your obligation to tell the truth and not to conceal anything prior to giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I may have forgotten something, because I was there for three years and I could tell you about that for ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was do you think one of the reasons it was given before a judge so that there would be no question but that you were advised to tell the truth and not conceal anything, and that it would therefore be an official statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that was the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other persons went with you and gave similar statements on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I was on my own, I had received a summons to appear. Maybe there was somebody there before me or after me, but while I was giving my statement, I was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone else that received such a summons and gave such a statement to this court in Visegrad regarding their experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were quite a few of them, all of those who had been in the Celebici camp and all the other camps, not just the Celebici camp. All over the place in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your impression was that this court was involved in conducting an investigation and took statements from a number of witnesses who had knowledge about Celebici and other camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they had conducted an investigation. I know that they took statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of other people you know who made statements to a court at the request of the Association of Detainees? Just those you know who did that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember those names now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not even one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe Spaso Miljevic was there, Grozdana Cecez and so forth, but I am not sure. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any statements made by any other persons to this court or any other court at the request of the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this information was not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Association of Detainees kept these statements that all these people were making to this court and perhaps other courts in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I just know where the Association is. I do not know where they keep the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been to the offices of the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you believe, you have a kind of sense, I guess, that Spaso Miljevic and Grozdana Cecez gave similar statement to the court. I would like you to think very carefully and tell us if you can give us the names of any more people who you think might have done so or who you know did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see them so I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with other detainees, did any of them tell you they had given such statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Mr. Draganic who you talked to last night? Did he say about making such a statement to the Association of Detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss that. I think he may have given a statement. I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anybody else that you think did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had given a statement to the Association of Detainees, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all those who are members of the Association of Detainees had given such statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it is a requirement that you give such a statement to become a member of the Association of Detainees, is it not? That is one of the things you have to do to become a member.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not a condition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, everyone who is a member of the Association did give such a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think yes, but it is enough for a person who have spent one day in a camp to become a member of the Association of Detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I am going to ask the Registrar to find some photographs and ask the usher to show them to you. (Pause). May I assist, your Honour? May I assist the Registry in finding the photographs I want?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can. You are really not too sure about the exhibit you are referring to. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence, your Honour. Mr. Kuljanin, I am showing you a couple of photographs and I would ask the usher to tell us what the exhibit numbers are on the back of them. The first one is a woman and that one is. THE USHER: D6/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It must be D4/2. The male is? THE USHER: D5/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: D5/2, okay. D6/2 and D5/2? THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would ask you, Mr. Kuljanin, to look at those photographs and tell us if you know either of those people pictured there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the woman who is depicted in that first photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Mrs. Dusica Bojic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is she?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who is she? She is the head of the documentation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What documentation centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the Association of Detainees in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever met with her personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is she the person that asked you to go to the court and make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean this court here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am talking about the court in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know who thought that, because I received a summons from the Visegrad court to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it is the Visegrad court knew that you had any information that would be of interest to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you discussed your experiences in Celebici with this woman shown in that first photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give her a statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she discuss with you the possibility of your coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We talked only about the camp. We did not talk, nor have I ever thought that she would have anything to do with this, because that is not her job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she record the conversation that you had with her about your experiences in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see that, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we understand that her job is head of the documentation centre, that would imply that her job is to document what happened in the camp, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, but I never had time to give any statements. I did not see her record anything. She may have recorded something, but secretly, but I do not think that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge at all of how it is she might have documented what you told her about your experiences in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on the basis of the statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement you are referring to is the one you gave to the court in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge the way this Association was documenting what had happened in Celebici and other camps was by having people go to the court and give formal statements to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the other photograph, will you please? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that? Excuse me, just a minute, do not answer that question. Do we have a protection issue with regard to that question? I will ask the Prosecutor before I ask you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know who it is, your Honour, so I cannot answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The person testified here as Witness O.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do now, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought you might. Can we go into private session for a moment, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we go into closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did this gentleman appear on Belgrade television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no idea, your Honour, but the situation is that we are not so much concerned about names being mentioned but names of them being mentioned as witnesses is what concerned us. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have told us this morning with regard to all of these statements, except perhaps the one that I showed you of, I think, 12th January 1993, with regard to the rest of them, you had an opportunity before this morning to look at them, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just like you did with Sabina Manke on November 14th 1996, you noticed what it was about those statements that was incorrect, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make notes, did you write down the things about each of those statements that were incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave a verbal correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you give that verbal correction to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the judge -- I mean to Mrs. Sabina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is since you have arrived here at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about since you have arrived here at The Hague? Have you had an opportunity to make any corrections since you have arrived here at The Hague or to tell anyone about things in those statements that you now contend were not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would that be that you have talked to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann sitting over there that questioned you earlier today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first of those occasions, how long did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes, not very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the second occasion how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same, maybe up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was a third occasion, how long that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the whole time that you have been here in The Hague, you have discussed these matters with Mr. Niemann for less than an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, an hour an hour and a half for the entire time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of that you had an opportunity to review all of these statements and to tell Mr. Niemann the things that were not correct in the statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any notes about the things that were not correct while you were here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Mr. Niemann, on the basis of my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Niemann was making notes but you were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone ask you to take all these statements back to your hotel with you, go through them and mark the parts of them that you thought were not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think we did that at the court itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question or two about the statement which you concede is true and completely true, that being the one that you gave to the court in Visegrad on February 3rd 1996, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in that statement, and I am going to quote the English version and I will go very slowly so that it can be translated to you: "At the beginning of June 1992, I was in the Serbian village of Cerici, near Konjic."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "When the Muslim armed forces attacked this village on 10th June 1992. I was captured, together with Miro Golubovic from Cerici."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "That same day, we were taken to Celebici camp."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you told the judge in Visegrad on 3rd February 1996, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not on the 10th but between the 6th and the 7th. That was when I was detained in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You then rather immediately after that gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, that being on 23rd February 1996, just 20 days later, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again I am going to read you part of that statement: "On 9th June 1992, a relative of mine, Miro Golubovic, and myself called the commander of the HVO military police, the Croat Darko Verkic, who used to be a great friend of mine personally."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but we did not invite him, he was invited by one of our men from the village, but following our initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I first started asking you questions, I asked you, Mr. Kuljanin, to pay particular attention to my questions, and that I would try to ask them in a way that could be answered either yes or no and that if I wanted you to explain, I would ask you to do that. All I am asking you right now is to confirm for us that these are the things you told the Office of the Prosecutor during your first statement to them on February 23rd 1996. Do we understand each other at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to continue now what this statement reflects that you told the Office of the Prosecutor: "We wanted to go to Serbia through Croatia, and wanted a pass for that. Darko himself came to get us on 10th June 1992. We drove in his police van, together with six or seven of his policemen from Cerici towards Celebici, to have what we believed a short informal interrogation there, and from there, we were supposed to continue to go on to Croatia." That is what you told the Office of the Prosecutor on February 23rd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was less than three weeks after you had given your statement to the court in Visegrad, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony before this court with regard to that moment of time right after you had arrived at Celebici, you described how you were first lined up, placed against building 22 and beaten, and then taken by Mr. Delic to the manhole accompanied by Mr. Verkic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think we understood each other quite well. There is a mistake here. I was beaten up after I had left the manhole and I was put against the wall of building number 22, and not when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your position then yesterday was you were not beaten upon your arrival at Celebici but taken rather directly to the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you gave on January 15th 1994, which you have had an opportunity to review, that statement reflects that you said the following: "We came to the gate of the Celebici prison where we were held for about five minutes as Verkic got out from the car to the registration desk and he talked about something with a guard. When he came back to the car, we continued further into the prison. After some 300 metres the vehicle stopped and Verkic got out. He approached a manhole with an iron cover which was locked with an Elzett padlock. I did not understand why he was opening the manhole. While I was sitting in the car, I thought it was some kind of a joke." You then went on to describe how he had ordered you into the manhole and how Miro Golubovic got in first and then you. Is that what you told the person who was questioning you on January 15th 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your contention here today that that statement is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On February 23rd 1996, you were interviewed by Sabina Manke of the Office of the Prosecutor, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told Ms. Manke, did you not, that on arrival at the camp you were attacked by Muslim policemen: "One attacked me with a knife and tore my jacket. Delic and a driver took me and my relative to the manhole." Is that what you told Ms. Manke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Ismet Hebibovic attacked me inside the van with a knife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the time at Celebici when you were taken for interrogation. Yesterday I believe what you told us was that you were taken from the manhole and taken to building 22 by Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were taken to building 22 and put up against the wall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, facing the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were beaten for about half an hour prior to being interrogated, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I stood for quite some time in front of the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your statement on 15th January 1994, which you have signed, says that you were removed from the manhole by Mucic, Verkic and "the Verkic guys", the HVO police, and taken for interrogation by Kuhar for a one hour interrogation. In that statement you said nothing about being beaten at building 22 prior to that statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I object to questions being asked about these statements which the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beat me again --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would just ask that the statements that the witness has attested to as having been taken under duress be not used for the purposes of impeachment. How can they possibly be the basis if an impeachment? If my friend is doing something other than impeaching the witness, I do not know, but if that is what his intention is, then in my submission these documents cannot be used for that basis, having regard to what the witness has attested to in the circumstances in which they have been obtained. I object to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what I have established and if it is not correct I will stand corrected, but I think what I have established was that on November 14th 1996 he was given an opportunity by Sabina Manke to state any corrections that he had to any of these statements and stated a few, which did not include the statement that you are referring to right at the present time. That is what I think the situation is. Even those he was not given an opportunity perhaps to correct them at the time they were made, he was given that opportunity by Sabina Manke on November 14th and made very few corrections, thereby implicitly verifying the balance of what was given in those statements. If I am wrong about that, I am wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is not the basis of the objection. The objection is the authorship, the freedom under which he was when he made this statement. I think that is what counsel is objecting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree with that. What I am saying is: if at a later point Ms. Manke showed him this statement and said "is there anything in this statement that you would like to change that is incorrect" and he said, "the date here is wrong, I will change that but nothing else", then he has independently verified that statement at a later date, whether he was allowed to see it at the time he made it or not. It is my contention that he has done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But he still has not been put to the question whether that statement was voluntarily made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will ask an additional question or two, your Honour. Maybe I can clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
